name: CRB-913

lead: CRB-913 is an experimental peripherally acting CB1 receptor blocker being studied for obesity. Fat-loss readers follow it as a possible add-on to GLP-1 drugs.

It acts as an inverse agonist at CB1, a receptor linked to appetite and metabolism. A 2023 paper in Obesity reported that in diet-induced obese mice it enhanced the weight loss from tirzepatide, semaglutide and liraglutide. A phase 1b trial (NCT07310901, 254 participants, started December 2025) is registered as completed, with no human results identified.

paras: It is available only in clinical trials, and the research pairs it with GLP-1 drugs.
Human safety data are not public. The earlier CB1 blocker rimonabant was withdrawn over psychiatric effects, and whether CRB-913 shares them has not been reported. It is not approved.

angle.text: CRB-913 is a CB1 blocker that lowers appetite and fat gain, followed by fat-loss readers as an add-on to GLP-1 drugs for a leaner look. It boosted weight loss in obese mice; human data are not yet public.

lead: CRB-913 is an investigational peripherally acting cannabinoid receptor 1 (CB1) inverse agonist being studied for obesity. It is not approved for any use.[1][2]

In a 2023 paper in Obesity, researchers reported that in diet-induced obese mice it enhanced the weight-loss efficacy of tirzepatide, semaglutide and liraglutide.[1] A Phase 1b trial in otherwise healthy participants with obesity (NCT07310901, 254 participants, started December 2025) is registered as completed.[2] No human results were identified in the sources reviewed.

paras: A 2-part Phase 1b study of safety, pharmacokinetics and efficacy in participants with obesity enrolled 254 people, began on 4 December 2025 and is listed as completed.[2] No results have been found.
The 2023 mouse study characterised CRB-913 as a CB1 inverse agonist and reported enhanced efficacy when added to three incretin drugs.[1] Mouse findings do not establish effects in humans.

timeline.event: Mouse study of CRB-913 with incretin drugs published.[1]
